reason: The sources provide numerous cross-verified, astonishing facts about Iapetus's two-toned color dichotomy, walnut shape, and massive equatorial ridge.
story: In 1671, astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini spotted a new moon orbiting Saturn, but whenever it crossed to the eastern side of the planet, it vanished completely. Cassini correctly deduced that the moon, Iapetus, was tidally locked and had one hemisphere vastly darker than the other. Centurions later, spacecraft confirmed his wild theory: Iapetus is the solar system's ultimate yin-yang world. Its leading face is pitch black like coal, while its trailing side gleams bright like ice. Because of its sluggish 79-day rotation, solar heating triggers a runaway thermal cycle where water ice evaporates from the dark terrain and freezes onto the colder bright regions, leaving behind a soot-thin coating of dark organics. Even weirder, wrapping around its equator is a colossal mountain ridge up to 12 miles high—taller than Mount Everest—giving this frozen world the bizarre, bulging appearance of a giant celestial walnut.
angle: Iapetus is a two-toned celestial walnut with one pitch-black face, one snow-white face, and a 12-mile-high mountain ridge girdling its equator.

claims.claim: Iapetus was discovered in 1671 by astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini.
Iapetus is the third-largest moon of Saturn.
Iapetus is tidally locked to Saturn, keeping the same face toward the planet.
Cassini could easily view Iapetus on the western side of Saturn, but it disappeared from view on the eastern side.
Cassini correctly deduced that Iapetus has one bright hemisphere and one dark hemisphere.
The leading hemisphere of Iapetus is extremely dark with an albedo of 0.03 to 0.05.
The trailing hemisphere of Iapetus is bright with an albedo of 0.5 to 0.6.
Iapetus takes approximately 79 days to complete both its rotation and its orbit.
The dark material covering the moon is a very thin layer only about one foot thick.
Thermal runaway sublimation drives ice from warmer dark regions to condense on colder bright areas.
Iapetus has an equatorial ridge of mountains running along its equator.
The equatorial ridge and bulging waistline give Iapetus the appearance of a walnut.
The equatorial ridge was discovered in Cassini spacecraft images taken on December 31, 2004.
Peaks along the equatorial ridge reach heights of up to 20 kilometers (12 miles) high.
Because its orbit is inclined relative to Saturn's ring plane, Iapetus is the only large moon with a clear view of Saturn's rings.
Geological features on Iapetus are named after characters and places from the epic poem The Song of Roland.
The dark region covering the leading hemisphere is named Cassini Regio.
Iapetus experiences massive, long-runout landslides known as sturzstroms.

disputed: Origin of the equatorial ridge: Sources present competing hypotheses, including ancient rapid spin freeze-out, collapse of an ancient debris ring, interior icy upwelling, or convective overturn. Scripts should present this as an unsolved mystery.

Initial darkening mechanism: Sources note theories ranging from Phoebe dust deposition to internal cryovolcanism; scripts should frame external dust sweep-up followed by thermal runaway as the prevailing model.

East versus West visibility in discovery: S7 claims Cassini saw Iapetus on the eastern side and lost it on the western side, whereas S1, S3, and S4 specify it was visible on the west and disappeared on the east. S7's inverted account should be left out.
